"Mysterious resort fees are the most dishonest charges in travel industry"

I got hit by one of these. Not a resort, but a room I booked on Expedia.

It was a last minute booking and the city was basically sold out. I was rushing and found a room for $300 a night. More than I wanted to spend, but I was in a crunch. When the invoice came, there was a $120 cleaning fee attached to it. That's almost half the cost of the room. At $420 a night, I could have stayed in a much better place and been pampered.

I went back to Expedia and sure enough, small print showed there was a cleaning fee. I just missed it because I focused on the big price on the page.

Oh yeah, also, no cancellations.

Bastards.

It was totally my fault, but I've never seen that before on Bookings.com or Expedia. I wasn't expecting it.

Best part - the room was dirty.

Such bullshit practice. The fact they are artificially deflating the price then tacking on fucking ridiculous fees. I wrote my representative and senator complaining about that practice. If enough noise is made, my hope is to put some pressure on "Big Travel" and reverse this nonsensical bullshit.

Like I said, it was ultimately my fault for not reading the webpage completely. It's scummy behaviour, but I'm fully to blame.

I left a nasty review because the accommodations didn't demand such high rates, the place was dirty, and I make to to note to other people using the website to check the cleaning fee. For Expedia customers, this will help the most.

Next time I just need to watch out for it. Although I usually use Booking.com, I will probably avoid Expedia all together for allowing this.
If I were you, I would just not sign the credit card receipt.
It was electronically processed and I took possession of the room. I can't fight it.

Sure you can. Call the credit card company, say you didn't agree to the charges when you booked the room, and you weren't going to sleep on the street that night. If it's Amex, it's darn-near a lock. Also file a BBB complaint against the hotel, complain to the AG, and make a stink. Figure out the CEO's own email address and send him a letter.

"This act of aggression will not stand, man." -The Dude

Indeed they are. I refuse to pay them. If I see an extra charge I didn't agree to upon checkout, I just won't sign the credit card receipt. They can try to charge me, but without a signed receipt, it ain't happening.

This is part of the reason I like to rough it instead of going to nice hotels and resorts and what not. I like actually speaking face to face with the hotel manager and making the deal there so a) I'm familiar with management and it feels more welcoming to me b) they can't sneakily charge me extra nor can they even try when I'm paying in cash and have an amount already calculated in my head from my agreed upon rate.

Obviously, my way isn't for everyone, but my experiences doing it that way have sometimes led to really, really, really amazing deals in some hidden gems.

Discuss below, if you have an idea for a future movie put it in the future movie thread here.

Personal favourite here so I'm not holding back.

Seldom does a film elucidate the culpability of our culture,of our society, in the mayhem and madness we often find in everyday life. According to Se7en, our culture is drifting through darkness. The mouthpiece for this thematic undercurrent is Somerset, a literate man who also happens to be a detective, a man who can read a clue ("This isn't going to be a happy ending") or Dante's Inferno with equal aplomb. He even provides the film's final thematic statement with a quote from Hemingway. His quirkiness, perhaps the outgrowth of a brilliant mind, is no worse than that of any prophet or seer of old, those harbingers of Biblical insight whom others always find kooky and offbeat. He is not well loved for his cynical, pessimistic outlook (such that his consuming motivation is to retire and get out of town). However, by the end it becomes clear that it is Somerset who sees our dark world with the prophet's particular clarity. (It is left to his partner Mills to find this out the hard way).

Working on us to reinforce this world as Somerset sees it is the film's astounding mise-en-scene, a disturbing film-noir setting developed by director David Fincher and cinematographer Darius Khondji. Flashlights barely illuminate the slimy walls of the roach-infested tenement of one victim and the dark bedroom of another. Rain pours down in buckets. Bird's-eye-view shots of downtown (the city is never named- a generic, everyman's kind of place) show dingy, sooty rooftops and grimy streets. Only the film's closing scene is in bright sunlight, which by then only serves as ironic counterpoint to what we see happening.

This is Somerset's vision; both inhabited and described by him. He finds a surprising fellow traveler in, not his partner, but the elusive killer John Doe. Doe shares the vision and provides an unsettling echo to the rumblings and teachings of Somerset. If one looks at life through the Somerset lens, one must admit that John Doe has a valid point. He and Somerset have arrived at the same conclusion, the difference between them being how they have responded. (Somerset longs to escape to some otherworldly realm in the country. Doe has taken action.)

Though gripping and fast moving, this is not an action film. It holds our interest through the workings of horror and mystery: a stark, film-noir detective piece. Except for one tense pursuit through halls and alleys in pouring rain, as well as the bit of ending action, there is surprisingly little violence. We see each murder, save two, after the fact, as a crime scene. This only makes the final act that much more suspenseful.

This is a very tight film. Elements within: dialogue, actions, lighting, setting, all of these tend to reinforce one another to paint a solid picture. It is a perverse logic that makes the final and seventh sin complete perfectly the circle of events begun with the first. What is life if not a vicious cycle?

SiaSL was the second book I latched on to (The first being Arthur C. Clarke's 2010).

Around the age of 10 I was put into remedial reading classes and summer school reading programs. All it was in the end was that I didn't like the drek they were giving us to read in school. As soon as I found sci-fi I read a book every few days, and particularly Clarke and Heinlein.

SiaSL was my first Heinlein book, which I read at 12. Loved it. It was just so rich and vibrant. As you've mentioned, Heinline had a way with words and his stories. They really take you for a ride, whereas, while I also love Clarke's books, they felt more restrained, and I always felt like I was riding a barely under control horse with Heinlein (And to some extent Herbert, and later again with Peter F. Hamilton).

An mildly interesting aside, my name is Peter M. Hamilton, and I have a poster from Peter F. Hamilton signed:

"From Peter Hamilton. To Peter Hamilton". :-)

This was one of the first books where I realized the purpose of sci-fi was to create a universe similar enough to ours to recognize, but different enough to criticize actual problems without offending everyone. I was born much later than the book came out but I imagine it caused a minor stir among the moralists.

I feel like I must be one of the great unwashed, but I really didn't like that book. It made me rather uncomfortable. I'm definitely not some sexually repressed Puritan, but he talked casually about promiscuity as if sexual fidelity was some kind of archaic concept that had no place in a rational society. It really bothered me. I got what he was saying, it just made me too uneasy to enjoy it for its philosophical ideas.

It's interesting that I a lot of people seem to take issue with the rationalised promiscuity in this book whereas I hear fewer complaints levelled at Iain M Banks' Culture novels in that regard. I suppose the difference is that much of the Culture's population is overtly hedonistic so it's easier for the reader to view the Culture negatively if they disapprove of its morality. And I suppose Banks doesn't dwell on it for long.

I've read SIASL repeatedly over the years. In my teens I thought it was brilliant, precisely because, as others said, Heinlein created a brilliantly complex world and clever storylines. As I got older and read more and more of his work though, I increasingly found that Heinlein's world view (his ultra-libetarian beliefs) clashed with what I believed. Re-reading SIASL a few years ago I could still enjoy the scope of the book and the storytelling, but the beliefs of Heinlein, as expressed through the character of Jubal, I found quite unacceptable. This is in part because Heinlein was writing at a particular time and place (and had a particular set of ideas) and in part because my own views had changed.

it is interesting though to read or re-read SIASL in the context of Heinlein's wider universe. Some of those novels are really dire (To Sail Beyond the Sunset being particularly awful, developing his particular obsession with incest). I still have a soft spot for Time Enough for Love though which doesn't fail as many of the Heinlein weirdness indicators as some of the others.

Stranger is less science fiction than philosophy fiction. The Martians have operationalized religion. Mike consequently doesn't need to feel anything for either murder or suicide. As Jubal notes this allows the Martian speakers to be gods and have moral structures in line with pagan pantheons. The final decision to spread the word in a Christian fashion become significant from this point of view.
I felt that the ending was a huge let down. I can't remember details right now, but I was so mad that it ended like that.

To me, the movie served as a reminder that we need to hang on to the things that are important to us, despite our advancing technology. We could live in a massively automated world, without becoming nothing more than tools of consumerism, and without destroying our planet, we simply have to care enough to make that choice. We need to advance our economy and our culture, along with technology, in order to truly take advantage of the benefits that our technological advances have to offer.

I didn't mean to sound like I'm against advancements, but that it's important to keep human connection and to make sure we don't let robots make the kinds of decisions humans should be making (the AI captain). Also, while some potential automations are a good idea on paper and in practice, some look good on paper, but could cost many people their jobs. So it's necessary that before we throw pieces of industries into the hands of automation, that we make sure we're not creating holes or whatever in the job market (i.e. I agree on "advancing our economy/culture along with technology"). For example, waiting tables helps many students through college, so if robots were to replace them, where would the people go for work? (Rhetorical.) Just lots of questions like this that would need to be seriously addressed in the face of expansive new automations.

I am entirely opposed, however, to over-automation of transportation, for both job and ethical reasons (let alone that I love cars and driving). Ethically, one main thing would be that manual override would be absolutely necessary (software does fail - it doesn't matter how rarely or often) and people would not be prepared (maybe not even trained) to take manual control, and would do something just out of instinct that would probably be wrong. (this happens when airplane autopilot systems fail and pilots pull up to maintain altitude, which doesn't work, instead of nose dip to maintain speed, which helps provide lift). I just am not comfortable with the idea of putting my life into the hands of software, rather than my own. I think the real answer to transportation safety is to have much, much more rigorous training for drivers licenses and have better public transit. Germany has this better system and about a third as many road fatalities per capita than the US and approximately 30,000 fewer total deaths in the most recent year data was collected [1]. The second main reason is privacy, and we know that's a whole thing of it's own that I won't get into.
